title: Recruiter

manager.name: Luis
manager.title: Head of People
manager.persona_note: Luis already knows someone who might fit. A good recruiter keeps the process fair for everyone, including that person.

teaser: Luis runs people at a clinic network and may already have someone in mind.
context: The company runs 20 health clinics and has about 300 staff.
The recruiter will hire for the clinics.
message: We need an in-house recruiter. I might know someone already.
The old ad is attached. Ten minutes?
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Luis will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to run. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to find nurses and clinic staff when they're hard to find.
needs.n2: Someone to set up and run the hiring software.

beats.label: A referral
beats.sam: A friend referred someone, Jesse, who sounds perfect. Can we skip the search?

choices.text: Jesse should definitely be considered. Would it be okay to put everyone through the same steps, so the decision feels solid?
choices.why: Welcoming the referral while keeping the process fair gives Jesse a real chance, and gives the manager confidence in the outcome.

choices.text: What makes Jesse sound like such a good fit?
choices.why: It's a fair question, but you haven't addressed the idea of skipping the search.

choices.text: Wouldn't skipping the search be unfair to other candidates?
choices.why: The point may be right, but put this way it sounds like an accusation.

beats.label: The comparison
beats.sam: So we don't need a long search, right?

choices.text: It doesn't need to be long. What would you want to compare Jesse against?
choices.reply: Someone who's hired a lot of nurses. That's our biggest pain.
choices.why: Asking what you'd compare against shows the real standard for the role.

choices.text: Should we keep it short, with just a couple of other people?
choices.why: Short is fine, but you still don't know what you're comparing against.

choices.text: Isn't a proper search needed to be fair?
choices.why: Pushing makes it feel like a fight, and the manager digs in.

choices.text: Which roles take the longest to fill right now?
choices.reply: Nurses. Some of those jobs sit open for four months.
choices.why: A follow-up on the hardest roles shows the skill you need to test for.

choices.text: Is it mostly office roles that are hard to fill?
choices.why: A leading guess gets a short no. An open question gets the real story.

choices.text: Why is hiring taking so long at the moment?
choices.why: It sounds like blame, and the manager gets defensive instead of telling you more.

beats.label: The software
beats.sam: They must know our hiring software.

choices.text: Who set it up, and how long did it take your team to learn it?
choices.reply: It's actually new to all of us.
choices.why: Checking a must-have against reality shows it's new to everyone.

choices.text: Got it. Should I screen for people who've used that exact system?
choices.why: It shrinks the search on a skill nobody on the team has yet.

choices.text: So the software is the most important skill?
choices.why: A leading question locked in a filter that doesn't fit the job.

beats.label: The pay
beats.sam: The pay is whatever the posting says.

choices.text: Is that range still current, or has it been updated?
choices.why: Checking whether an old number is still current keeps the search realistic for everyone.

choices.text: Okay. Should I use the posting range when I talk to candidates?
choices.why: Agreeing is easy, but an old range may be out of date.

choices.text: Aren't posted ranges usually out of date?
choices.why: A broad claim about their posting costs goodwill. Simply asking would have checked it kindly.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Clinic days
beats.sam: They'd be in a clinic two days a week.

choices.text: Being close to the clinics makes sense. What happens on those clinic days, so I can describe it to candidates?
choices.reply: They meet the clinic managers, sit in on interviews, and see what the jobs are really like.
choices.why: Accepting a reasonable request, then asking what happens on those days, shows curiosity and gives you a real selling point for candidates.

choices.text: Is there flexibility on the clinic days for the right person?
choices.reply: Not really. That's where the work is.
choices.why: It's a fair question, but asked before you understand why those days matter, it can sound like you're already negotiating against the manager.

choices.text: Most recruiters I talk to want to be fully remote. Could we drop the clinic days?
choices.why: Pushing to change a settled decision, with nothing to back it up, spends goodwill you'll need for the questions that actually change the search.

beats.label: How it's done
beats.sam: Recruiting is mostly posting jobs, really.

choices.text: Posting works for some roles. For nurses, what's worked best for you before?
choices.reply: Calling nurses directly, and asking our staff for referrals.
choices.why: Acknowledging what's true, then asking what works for the hard roles, shows the skill that matters.

choices.text: Which job boards do you usually post on?
choices.why: It's a question, but it keeps the job small. Asking about the hard roles would get further.

choices.text: So I should look for people who are good at writing job posts?
choices.why: Agreeing means you'd hire for posting jobs, which is the wrong skill for hard-to-fill roles.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: It's a pretty normal recruiter job.

choices.text: What would make a great recruiter want this job?
choices.reply: Every hire keeps a clinic open for patients.
choices.why: Asking what makes the job attractive gives you a meaningful pitch.

choices.text: So should I keep the description fairly standard?
choices.why: That undersells the job, which puts off the strongest people.

choices.text: Is anything really normal in healthcare recruiting?
choices.why: Questioning the manager rarely changes their mind. A question about the job does.

candidates.name: Kim
facts: Cut time to fill from 4 months to 6 weeks

reason.n1: Hires nurses fast by reaching out directly, which is the clinics' biggest pain.

view.n1: Kim would empty our open jobs list.

candidates.name: Darcy
facts: Writes job posts that attract lots of applicants

reason.n1: Has filled nursing roles, but through postings and agency lists. Luis said what works is calling nurses directly and asking for referrals.

view.n1: Darcy waits for applicants. Ours don't apply.

reason.n1: Knowing the software matches the old ad, but it's new to everyone, and Lane hasn't hired nurses.

view.n1: Lane knows the system, not the people we need.

candidates.name: Jesse
facts: Referred by a friend of Luis

reason.n1: The referral Luis had in mind. Bright and well regarded, but has hired office staff, not nurses. The fair process shows the gap.

view.n1: Jesse could grow into it. Not yet.
